title: KYC, CIP, and Identity Verification Flows

questions.question: A payouts platform verifies each seller's bank account with a micro-deposit and stores is_verified = true. Why is that not enough to meet a customer identification requirement?
options: Micro-deposits are too slow; regulators require identity to be verified in real time
It proves control of an account, not who the person is, and records no method or evidence
Bank accounts can be closed later, so verification must be repeated before every payout
Micro-deposit amounts are floats, so the stored verification result is not reliable
questions.explanation: CIP requires collecting identifying information (name, DOB, address, ID number in the US) and verifying the person, with records of the method and result. A micro-deposit proves control of a bank account only, and a bare boolean records nothing an examiner can rely on. Real-time verification is not required; the rule allows a reasonable time.

questions.question: Which statement correctly separates CIP from CDD?
options: CIP establishes and verifies identity; CDD adds purpose, risk profile, owners, and monitoring
CIP applies to individual customers; CDD applies only to legal-entity business customers
CIP is the US term and CDD the EU term for the same identity verification requirement
CIP happens at account opening; CDD happens only after a suspicious activity report
questions.explanation: CIP answers 'is this a real person and is it this person'; CDD builds on it with the nature and purpose of the relationship, a risk profile, beneficial owners for entities, and ongoing monitoring. The entity-only distractor confuses CDD with its beneficial-ownership element; CDD applies to every customer.

questions.question: Company A is owned 60% by Holding B and 20% directly by Zara. Zara also owns 20% of Holding B. Under a 25% ownership prong, is Zara a beneficial owner of A?
options: No, because neither her direct 20% nor her indirect stake reaches 25% on its own
No, because indirect stakes held through an entity are not counted for ownership
Yes, because she holds shares at two levels, which always triggers identification
Yes, because her direct 20% plus 0.60 x 20% indirect gives 32% effective ownership
questions.explanation: Effective ownership multiplies along each path and sums across paths: 20% + 0.60 x 20% = 32%, above the threshold. Evaluating each edge separately is the classic implementation bug that misses her. Indirect ownership is explicitly counted under both US and EU rules.

questions.question: The document-verification vendor is down for two hours. What should the onboarding state machine do with new applicants?
options: Approve them at full limits and re-verify them later, so that conversion is protected
Reject them with a request to try again, since verification cannot be completed now
Hold them in Verifying, or a restricted tier with low limits, and resume when it recovers
Skip the document step and rely on email and phone checks for applicants in that window
questions.explanation: The state machine fails closed: applicants wait in a pending state or get restricted access whose limits match the assurance actually achieved. Approving at full limits fails open and creates exactly the unverified accounts the rules prohibit; rejecting outright loses good customers for an internal outage.

questions.question: An engineer proposes storing full Aadhaar numbers and passport scans in the main customer table so support agents can see them. What is the right design?
options: Keep them in the main table but encrypt that column, so that support agents can still see them
Hold raw identifiers and documents in a vault, give other services tokens and masked values
Delete them right after verification, because privacy law forbids keeping identity documents
Store only a SHA-256 hash of each identifier, which satisfies record-keeping and privacy rules
questions.explanation: An identity vault isolates raw identifiers (UIDAI requires a vault with reference keys and masked display for Aadhaar) while other systems hold tokens, last-4 values, and verification outcomes. Deleting immediately breaks CIP record-keeping, which requires a description of the document for five years after closure; a bare hash of a low-entropy ID number is reversible by brute force and does not preserve the required description.

questions.question: An approved customer's name appears on a sanctions list update published today. Which onboarding design handles this correctly?
options: Nothing happens until the customer's scheduled periodic review, as screening is at onboarding
The customer is deleted from the system, along with balances, to remove the prohibited party
An alert is emailed to compliance, and the account stays fully active until someone replies
A rescreen raises an event that moves the account to Restricted, freezes funds, logs evidence
questions.explanation: Sanctions screening is continuous: every list update rescreens the base, and a confirmed match is a prohibition that must take effect immediately through the state machine, with funds blocked and the evidence logged. Waiting for periodic review leaves a prohibited party transacting; deletion destroys required records and the blocked funds must be held and reported, not removed.
